description: Somos estudantes de Engenharia da UEA e membros da Vento Norte UEA, a primeira equipe de foguetemodelismo da região Norte.
summary: What we developed was a desktop application (Electron + React) that works as an onboard assistant so astronauts can follow their own health with autonomy from Earth by using wearable technology—specifically, a smart ring. It addresses the following problem: creating a visual tool that allows astronauts to access and monitor their health data while aboard the spacecraft—a hostile environment with few people and extremely low gravity, which causes damage to various parts of the body. This is important because building an intuitive, functional interface to visualize crew health data by mission status requires a deep understanding of NASA teams and their work culture—one that always prioritizes team collaboration and the critical role of self-care. By that, we mean delivering a solution that turns real-time biometric data into clear, actionable insights, empowering the crew to take care of themselves and each other during the mission.
details:
Vento Norte Health is an offline health monitoring desktop application designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It allows crew members to log and track three critical health metrics — blood pressure, blood glucose, and body weight — using equipment already present on spacecraft (sphygmomanometer, glucometer, and SLAMMD/BMMD for microgravity weight measurement).

How it works

Each astronaut logs readings manually or through quick entry. The app applies color-coded alert rules: readings within normal range are shown in green, borderline values trigger an attention alert, and critical values notify the mission captain. All data is stored locally with no internet connection required, ensuring it works even during communication blackouts with Earth.

Benefits

The app puts health awareness directly in the astronaut's hands, in plain language, in 7 languages (Portuguese, English, Spanish, French, Russian, Japanese, and Mandarin). A gamification system rewards consistent health habits — not perfect values — through points, levels, badges, and team goals, reducing the psychological burden of long missions.

Intended impact

To reduce preventable health deterioration during deep-space missions by making self-monitoring simple, habit-forming, and accessible to non-medical crew members.

Tools and technologies used:

Electron, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Tremor, Recharts, Vitest (353 automated tests), JavaScript — all open source. Health range references were drawn from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), specifically the Inspiration4 civilian astronaut dataset (OSD-569), and the NASA Human Research Program risk protocols.

Creativity

Instead of building another clinical dashboard, the team focused on the astronaut's daily experience — quick logging, habit streaks, mood tracking, food diary, and a captain's panel for mission oversight. The privacy system gives each crew member three levels of data visibility, respecting personal boundaries while keeping the captain informed when it matters.
